paper_metadata.title: Enhanced fill probability estimates in institutional algorithmic bond trading using statistical learning algorithms with quantum computers

summary: The paper tests a 109‑qubit projected quantum feature map (PQFM) on IBM Heron processors for corporate bond RFQ fill‑probability prediction using 216‑feature market state vectors from 143,912 trading events. Classical ML models using hardware‑generated quantum features achieve median AUC up to 0.97 ± 0.02 versus ≈0.63 ± 0.04 with classical features (≈34% relative improvement), while noiseless quantum simulation performs slightly worse than classical features.

experiments.description: Projected quantum feature map (PQFM) generation with a Heisenberg-ansatz circuit on IBM quantum hardware and noiseless simulation, used as an offline feature transform for corporate bond RFQ fill-probability estimation; evaluated with classical ML backtesting on transformed features.

algorithm.variant: Projected Quantum Feature Map (PQFM) using a Heisenberg ansatz; compared shorter (1 block) vs longer (2 blocks) circuits

hyperparameters.observable_set: 1-local Pauli strings (X,Y,Z) on each qubit; some 2-local observables also included

algorithm.parameter_initialization: Random initial state for each qubit; random seed set to 0
algorithm.hyperparameters.observable_set: Primarily 1-local Pauli strings (X,Y,Z) on each qubit giving q = 3N = 327 observables for N=109 qubits; some additional 2-local Pauli strings may be included

problem_formulation.encoding_details: 216 normalized classical event features are scaled to [-1,1] and embedded into a 109-qubit Heisenberg-ansatz circuit; features are distributed across qubits and Trotter steps/blocks, then measured as Pauli expectations
problem_formulation.objective_function: Generate transformed feature vectors x' = $M(U_α(x)|b0⟩) to improve downstream fill-probability estimation for RFQ acceptance prediction
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: No explicit optimization constraints; classical-quantum event matching used later to reuse generated features for similar events
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: Heisenberg Hamiltonian H = Σ_j J_j [X_jX_{j+1} + Y_jY_{j+1} + 2Z_jZ_{j+1}] with Trotterized unitary evolution

problem_instance.description: Corporate bond RFQ fill-probability estimation on real intraday algorithmic trading data from HSBC; quantum features generated from market-state vectors and used in downstream ML models
problem_instance.dataset_name: HSBC corporate bond RFQ trading dataset

dataset_specification.description: Single representative sample of 16,000 events drawn from the active trading window (not per day)

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Classical features normalized by mean/std, then transformed with 2r*tanh(1/3) to reduce outliers and fit rotation ranges; event values scaled to [-1,1]; discretized into bins for classical-quantum event matching
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Backtesting over rolling time windows; out-of-sample AUC evaluated for blinding windows from 0 to 4 trading days; median test AUC reported across model/data configurations

noise_model.error_mitigation_method: Pauli Twirling and TREX (Twirled Readout Error eXtinction)

implementation_details.classical_solver: Qiskit Aer Estimator Primitive (noiseless simulation) used only for PQFM generation comparison; downstream evaluation uses classical ML models (LR, XGB, RF, NN)
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Feature normalization, outlier compression via tanh transform, binning for event matching, grouped PQFM unification by K identifier
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Backtesting with AUC metric; comparison of classical-input vs quantum-generated-input models; classical-quantum event matching to reuse PQFM features for similar events

speedup_claims.baseline_method: classical-input models and noiseless-simulation PQFM models
speedup_claims.conditions: out-of-sample test AUC on corporate bond RFQ fill-probability backtesting; hardware-generated PQFM features; up to 4 trading days of blinding
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a performance uplift in AUC, not a computational speedup; paper states no generalization guarantees and no causal explanation.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not defined; no asymptotic complexity comparison provided
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Unknown; the paper reports empirical AUC improvements but provides no algorithmic complexity analysis or scaling study
limiting_factors: No complexity or scaling analysis of PQFM vs classical feature transforms
Advantage measured only as ML accuracy improvement, not computational efficiency
Requires embedding 216 classical features into 109‑qubit circuits for each sample
Results depend strongly on hardware noise effects that are not theoretically understood
Classical ML models still perform the core prediction task

notes: Circuit depth was not explicitly given as a single depth number; only circuit structure is described (109 qubits, 1 or 2 blocks, Heisenberg ansatz, Trotterized unitary).
Speedup order is not claimed; paper reports empirical AUC uplifts only, so no asymptotic speedup is established.
The authors report up to 34% improvement in AUC using hardware-generated PQFM features but explicitly state they do not claim theoretical speedup or advantage.
Improvement is attributed partly to hardware noise characteristics rather than a provable quantum algorithmic benefit.

experiments.description: Projected quantum feature map generation on noiseless quantum simulation (Qiskit Aer / MPS) for the same corporate bond RFQ fill-probability task, used to compare against hardware-generated features.

algorithm.variant: Projected Quantum Feature Map (PQFM) using a Heisenberg ansatz on noiseless simulator
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Random initial state for each qubit; random seed set to 0

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Same 216-feature market-state vectors embedded into 109-qubit PQFM circuit and measured as Pauli expectations
problem_formulation.objective_function: Generate transformed features x' for downstream fill-probability estimation
problem_formulation.problem_hamiltonian: Heisenberg Hamiltonian with Trotterized unitary evolution

problem_instance.description: Same HSBC corporate bond RFQ dataset and active trading window as hardware experiment, but using noiseless simulation to generate PQFM features
problem_instance.dataset_name: HSBC corporate bond RFQ trading dataset

dataset_specification.description: European corporate bond market; same preprocessing and event matching as hardware experiment

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Normalization, tanh scaling, binning/event matching, PQFM feature extraction from simulator
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Same backtesting protocol and AUC evaluation as hardware experiment

implementation_details.classical_solver: Classical ML models (LR, XGB, RF, NN) for downstream evaluation

speedup_claims.caveats: No computational speedup is claimed; this experiment is a noiseless simulation baseline for feature generation.

limiting_factors: Noiseless quantum-simulation PQFM features produce slightly worse AUC than classical features
Simulation still requires full classical computation of the quantum circuit

notes: Noiseless simulator is explicitly described; Qiskit Aer and MPS are reported.
Circuit depth not explicitly quantified; only blocks and ansatz structure are given.
No asymptotic speedup claim is made.
Figure 10 shows noiseless simulation PQFM models achieving ≈0.60 AUC versus ≈0.63 for classical features, indicating classical baseline performs better.

experiments.description: Reproducibility tests of the same PQFM circuits executed on additional IBM Heron‑processor quantum hardware devices (ibm_fez and ibm_marrakesh) to validate whether the observed hardware‑noise‑induced performance gains persist across systems.

algorithm.variant: Projected Quantum Feature Map (PQFM) with Heisenberg ansatz (same circuits as main experiment)

key_results: Median test AUCs reproduced across devices with differences ≤1%
Same qualitative performance improvement observed on ibm_fez and ibm_marrakesh compared with classical and noiseless simulation features
